title: Angoff Standard-Setting for AI Safety Cutoffs

original_idea.body:
# Angoff Standard-Setting for AI Safety Cutoffs: Using Expert Panels to Define Meaningful Pass/Fail Thresholds on Safety Benchmarks

**Problem:** AI safety benchmarks currently use arbitrary numeric cutoffs (e.g., 80% refusal rate = 'safe') with no principled justification for why those thresholds represent meaningful safety distinctions. There is no structured method for translating benchmark scores into defensible deployment decisions.

**Direction:** Convene a structured Angoff panel of AI safety researchers who each estimate, item by item on an existing safety benchmark (e.g., MLCommons AI Safety v0.5 or StrongREJECT), the probability that a 'minimally safe' model would answer correctly. Average these estimates across panelists to derive a principled cutoff score. Analyze inter-panelist agreement (intraclass correlation), compare the resulting threshold to current ad hoc cutoffs, and examine whether the Angoff-derived cutoff changes deployment recommendations for existing model evaluations. Run the exercise with two panels (safety researchers vs. AI ethicists) and compare results as a convergent validity check.

**Why it matters:** Without principled standard-setting, AI safety thresholds are arbitrary and legally/ethically indefensible. Angoff panels have been used for decades in high-stakes credentialing (medical licensing, bar exams) to produce defensible cutoffs. Importing this methodology would make AI safety thresholds transparent, reproducible, and grounded in expert judgment rather than convention.

**Relevant context:** The MLCommons AI Safety Benchmark v0.5 explicitly acknowledges that determining cutoffs is an open problem. The contrasting groups and Angoff methods are both well-validated in clinical skills assessment literature (PMC12409087). Educational measurement R tools (eatATA, mirt) support the analysis. No prior work appears to have used structured standard-setting methodology for AI safety benchmark thresholds.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: arbitrary safety thresholds undermine regulatory and deployment decisions, and principled Angoff-derived cutoffs directly address this. Every link is explicit: arbitrary threshold -> meaningless pass/fail -> unsafe deployments. Principled thresholds are immediately actionable.

low_compute.reasoning: No compute needed. The method is expert panel judgment, statistical analysis of agreement (ICC), and comparison of thresholds. CPU-only R analysis.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: The Angoff method itself is conceptually simple (experts estimate probabilities). Organizing panels and computing ICC is intermediate. The main challenge is recruiting panelists, not technical complexity.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Requires recruiting expert panels, running the Angoff exercise, and computing agreement statistics. The logistics of panel recruitment make this a sustained effort, though a single-panel exercise on one benchmark is feasible.

quick_reasoning: Targets a specific, well-defined AI safety governance problem (principled deployment thresholds) with clear Angoff methodology; safety relevance is obvious and directly actionable for regulators.
